sections.heading: Pro Milone
paragraphs: Delivered (or rather, prepared - Cicero never actually gave this speech in the intimidating form we have it, and published a revised version afterwards) in 52 BC, Pro Milone defends Titus Annius Milo against a charge of murdering his political rival Publius Clodius Pulcher in a roadside brawl on the Appia. It is one of Cicero's most celebrated forensic speeches, prized for its argumentative construction as much as its (ultimately unsuccessful) defence.

The text here is Latin only, verbatim. Nothing is translated, modernised, normalised or silently corrected beyond the documented resolution of the source's own critical-apparatus markup (see "How it was imported" below). Where the source is irregular or a genuine judgement call was made, it is preserved/recorded and flagged in "Known gaps & anomalies" below.

sections.heading: No English edition bundled - by design
paragraphs: No English translation of Pro Milone is bundled alongside this Latin text. This is a deliberate choice, not an oversight: two independent research passes searched Perseus's own CTS catalog for this work (which lists no "perseus-eng*" English witness for phi0474.phi031), English Wikisource, and Project Gutenberg, and found no public-domain, complete digital English translation that meets this app's two-source verification policy. A handful of 19th-century (Yonge-tradition) translation leads exist only on the Internet Archive, outside this app's established two-source policy for translation-hunting, and were not independently verified for completeness - so they were not used. Rather than ship an unverified or partial English text, the decision was to publish the Latin text on its own, mirroring how this library already handles Aristotle's Physics (data/physics-grc) when no suitable public-domain translation could be confirmed. A future contributor who locates and verifies a suitable source is welcome to add a companion data/pro-milone-en/ work following the same flat section shape defined in data/pro-milone-la/types.ts.

sections.heading: The edition
paragraphs: The printed source, per this XML file's own <teiHeader>/<sourceDesc> and __cts__.xml, is Albert Curtis Clark, ed., M. Tulli Ciceronis Orationes, Vol. 6 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1918) - part of the Scriptorum Classicorum Bibliotheca Oxoniensis (Oxford Classical Texts) series (the same volume that also contains Pro Marcello and Pro Ligario, both also bundled in this app).

The oration is divided into 105 numbered sections (the modern citation unit, e.g. "Mil. 79") and, more coarsely, 38 traditional Roman-numeral "chapters" (e.g. "Mil. xxix"), both printed in this source; see "Reference scheme" below for how each is represented here.

sections.heading: Digital source
paragraphs: The machine-readable text is the TEI/EpiDoc XML file phi0474.phi031.perseus-lat2.xml (CTS urn:cts:latinLit:phi0474.phi031.perseus-lat2) from the Perseus Digital Library / OpenGreekAndLatin canonical-latinLit repository. It is fetched once (and cached under the importer's own raw/ directory) and bundled with the app; nothing is loaded from the network at runtime.

sections.heading: How it was imported
paragraphs:
The importer slices the single
body into its 105 flat, numbered
divisions (there is no intervening Book/Chapter tier), then takes the

paragraph(s) inside each section (joined with a blank line if more than one) as that section's single Passage. Clark's apparatus criticus (, 583 occurrences) is excluded entirely, tag and content. This witness carries no at all (unlike Pro Sestio's 3). Two tr. tribunum-style pairs (both "tr. pl." for "tribunum plebis") are resolved to their reading - what Clark's edition actually prints as running text - with the literal abbreviation dropped, matching this library's established choice/sic/corr convention. (Clark's regularised-spelling form), (his own editorial addition), (a numeral set in small capitals), and (short quoted/reported speech within Cicero's own oration) are all unwrapped and kept inline, verbatim. The work-level running-title is discarded (not a section heading). Entities are decoded and runs of whitespace collapsed; the words are otherwise untouched.

The source also prints the oration's traditional chapter citation inline, as <milestone unit="chapter" n="N"/> markers (38 total, sequential). Each section's Division.ref is set to the chapter number active at that section's start - the nearest preceding milestone in document order - built by a single left-to-right pass that never looks ahead; see "Reference scheme" below.

sections.heading: Reference scheme
paragraphs: Citation here is by section (Division.id "sec-N" / Division.number "N", e.g. "Mil. 79") - the same numbering the source itself prints and the modern standard citation unit for this speech - plus, in Division.ref, the traditional chapter number (e.g. "29") active at that section's start, reconstructed from the source's own inline chapter milestones. sec-1's ref is null: the source's own chapter-1 milestone sits just inside sec-1's own text, not before it, so no chapter has yet begun when sec-1 opens - the one documented, expected case of a null ref in this work. Passage.ref is null throughout and Passage.n is "" throughout (no further printed sub-numbering survives in this source).

sections.heading: Known gaps & anomalies
paragraphs: Every irregularity is either preserved verbatim and flagged, or excluded with the exclusion explicitly documented; anomalies.json records the full machine-readable list.

Apparatus criticus resolved into a single reading text. 583 <note> elements were excluded entirely as scholarly commentary, not counted individually. This witness has zero <del> (unlike Pro Sestio's 3). 6 <add> elements (Clark's own editorial additions) were kept inline. Two <choice>/<abbr>/<expan> pairs (both "tr. pl.") were resolved to their expanded reading, the literal abbreviation dropped.

Completeness. All 105 sections and all 38 chapter milestones are present and in sequential order, from the incipit "etsi vereor, iudices, ne turpe sit pro fortissimo viro dicere incipient..." to the explicit "...optimum et sapientissimum et fortissimum quemque delegit."
